title: Building and Maintaining Team Morale- Introduction to Field Leadership Section - 1
Chapter 0 - Introduction to Critical Leadership Training

vtt.text: How well do you handle your emotions? Are you at the mercy of them or can you use them to your advantage? And what about when it comes to others? Can you recognize how the people around you are feeling? Leaders with high emotional intelligence are skilled at identifying, understanding, and managing their emotions and the emotions of others. They can tune into how they're feeling, and regulate their reactions. And with that self-understanding, they can also better recognize and respond to the feelings of others. It's an important skill to have, so let's take a look at the two categories of emotional intelligence and why they're necessary for leadership success. The first category of emotional intelligence is personal competence, which refers to how well you recognize and manage your emotions. It's made up of three elements: self-awareness, self-regulation, and self-motivation. Self-awareness is being aware of your emotions, it's recognizing your feelings, understanding why they're happening, and noticing how your thoughts and behaviors are affected. Self-regulation refers to how well you handle your emotions. It revolves around self-control, thinking before you act, and maintaining resilience during difficult times. Finally, self-motivation refers to your personal drive. It's using your emotions as a mobilizing tool to ensure you stick to your goals. The second category of emotional intelligence is social competence which helps you build strong social relationships and create meaningful interactions. Social competence is defined as how well you recognize and manage the emotions of others. It involves two elements, empathy and social skills. Empathy is understanding another's emotions, it's looking outside your perspective and seeing things from another's point of view. Social skills refer to how well you interact with others, it's taking your understanding of another's feelings and using that knowledge to create positive interactions. So, emotional intelligence is just as much about knowing yourself as it is about knowing others and it plays an essential role in the quality of your leadership. Here are four leadership benefits of high emotional intelligence. The first leadership benefit of emotional intelligence is that you're more likely to make objective decisions. Emotion-filled decisions are often shortsighted and risky, but if you can recognize your feelings, you'll know when they're getting in the way of your actions. Second, you can expect fewer blind spots as you'll be more aware of your internal and external reality. When it comes to you, you'll think before you act and be less likely to jump to conclusions. And when it comes to others, you'll notice when employees are struggling and you'll know how to give them the support they need. Third, your communication will be more effective, you'll know how to control your emotions, communicate constructive messages, engage your staff's understanding, plus when listening to your team, you'll observe their reactions and be more likely to understand where they're coming from. Finally, a leader with high emotional intelligence can improve workplace morale. You can better gauge how subordinates are feeling and address those emotions with kindness and warmth. You'll understand the nuances of various situations and bring positivity into the workplace, thus boosting employee happiness. To succeed as a leader, you need more than just intellectual smarts, you also need emotional intelligence. So, keep the benefits in mind and make an effort to start tuning into your emotions, practicing self-regulation, and finding ways to cultivate internal motivation. Then, look outside yourself to develop empathy and improve your social skills. Follow these tips and you can reap long-term rewards both inside and outside the office.
